text: A man has decided the world outside is contaminated, and no one in his household will be permitted to test the claim. Arturo Ripstein films the consequences from inside: a house in Mexico, 1971, where the father sets the hours, assigns the work, and calls the arrangement protection. The children have grown up in it, with a street they can hear and are not allowed to enter. What the 110 minutes watch is the maintenance - the daily labour of keeping a doctrine standing while the people inside it turn into adults with appetites of their own. The father's own hunger runs the same engine as his rule. Ripstein keeps the argument at floor level, in chores and timetables. Domestic order here stands for nothing else; it is a job somebody performs, at a cost he charges to everybody else.

The shoe factory is the point of the fraud: it has to exist on paper and never open. Fiore and his apprentice Gino land in Albania just after the Communist state falls, needing an Albanian name at the head of the company, and they find one in Spiro - old, confused, lately out of prison, cheap. Spiro's signature is the only asset the company has. Then Fiore goes back to Italy for the subsidy and Spiro walks off. Gianni Amelio turns the rest into a search across roads and ports crowded with people trying to move the other way, toward Italy, until Gino's passport looks less like an advantage than a thing he is carrying. The film took the European Film Award for Best Film. Long before it ends, the con is the least interesting business in the frame.

A lawyer loses a case he should have won, and the woman who trusted him goes to prison. What Jack Ng Wai-Lun builds from that is a Hong Kong courtroom picture with 133 minutes to spend, most of it on unglamorous machinery: who was paid, which document went unread, how a wealthy family's account of events becomes the account a court hears. At that length there is room for the client's side too, the time she spends inside while the case is rebuilt. The genre pleasures are all in place - the cross-examination, the reversal, a barrister's mouth used as a weapon. Underneath them sits a harder proposition, that the original failure was ordinary carelessness by a man good at his job and not paying attention. Restitution here is procedural. It is filed, argued, and paid for in hours.

The town is small enough that a rumour has to be walked past every day. John Duigan sets his story in rural Australia in 1962, near enough to the present for the adults to still be enforcing the rules they were raised under, and puts at its centre a boy whose body has not caught up with what he feels. His closest friend since childhood is a girl further along than he is. She turns toward a rugby player with a reputation, and the boy does what the very young do, which is watch, interpret, and get it partly right. Duigan lets the humiliation last. A small town keeps its records by mouth, and does not correct them. Nothing gets promoted into tragedy; the currency is a look held too long across a schoolyard, and a house that a story attached itself to and stayed.

October 2, 1968 is the date the film takes, and it was made in Mexico twenty-one years afterward. Jorge Fons allows himself 96 minutes and a single day, in which a student demonstration meets soldiers who have been issued live rounds. It is filed as a thriller, and the label is not wrong: the suspense is built out of an outcome the audience already knows and the hours that precede it. The compression is the method - no panorama of a decade, no explanatory prologue, only the time in which ordinary people learn what their government is prepared to do to them and then have to decide, one at a time, what happens next. Rojo amanecer was named best picture at the Ariel awards. Twenty-one years is not a long interval when a share of the audience was standing there.

The arithmetic is the trap: for one girl to be let go, another has to be brought in. Sofia is fourteen and in love with Ulises, which is the entire mechanism required to move her into a prostitution network in Mexico, and the same mechanism is the only thing that could move her out, at the price of a stranger her own age. David Pablos, working from a Jorge Volpi novel, builds the film around that exchange rather than around a rescue. It runs 105 minutes at the level of rooms and errands, and its worst moments are transactions. Nobody here is a monster by trade. They are boyfriends and brothers and neighbours with a quota to meet, and the attention stays on how unremarkable the conversations sound once affection has already done the preparatory work.

Five short films, made in 2015, each guessing at what Hong Kong would be in 2025. The guesses are not consoling: residents and activists under crackdown, a government that has stopped negotiating, ordinary rooms in which the rules have quietly changed. Dystopia is usually set far enough ahead to be safe; a decade is not that far. The anthology form suits the material, since the pieces stand apart from one another and the dread accumulates across the gaps rather than building inside any single story. It took Best Film at the Hong Kong Film Awards, which for a set of low-budget shorts says something about the room it played to. The year it was imagining has now arrived and gone. That does something to the film nobody involved could have arranged.

Ash falls on the house all day, from the cane fields that press against it on every side. Alfonso comes back after seventeen years because his son is gravely ill, and finds the household still running without him: the woman who was once his wife, a daughter-in-law, a grandson, and the crop closing in on the yard. César Augusto Acevedo shot it at 97 minutes and it moves at the speed of the work - burning, waiting, wages, water. The ash is not weather; it is somebody's harvest, burning on schedule. The Caméra d'Or went to it, and what earns that is the refusal to turn an old man's return into a reconciliation drama: he is a pair of hands offered late to people who arranged their survival around his absence.

A boy needs help with a car he has already crashed, and everybody he asks is busy with something else. Fernando Eimbcke gives that errand 89 minutes and declines to make it larger: knocking on doors, waiting, being handed conversation instead of a repair, moving on to the next person who is glad to talk and slow to act. Mexico, 2008, and the town gives him time he did not ask for. Filed as comedy and drama both, it earns the first through duration - a shot held a beat past where it would ordinarily be cut, until awkwardness turns funny and then turns into something quieter. Stalling is the boy's method as much as the film's. A car needs fixing and a day needs filling, and only one of those is a job for a mechanic.

The new neighbour is a radio announcer, and he has brought a voice trained to fill a room and a high opinion of himself. Shirley Barrett sets him down in an Australian country town where two sisters live close enough to hear each other's business, and the crush that follows is less a romance than a contest neither will admit to entering. Scale is the joke. Two sisters, one town, one available man with a microphone. A person of very small consequence becomes the most consequential thing on offer, and the sisters rearrange their lives around him with a seriousness the film neither mocks nor saves them from. It keeps a straight face as the behaviour gets stranger, holding off a long while on whether the man is ridiculous or something worse.

Cans and bottles, collected after a restaurant shift, are part of how the rent gets paid. Or is seventeen or eighteen, still at school, and has organised her days around a mother lately out of hospital: a cleaning job lined up, a flat kept in order, the Tel Aviv streets where Ruthie used to work made as unnecessary as one teenager can make them. Keren Yedaya films this as labour rather than melodrama, and the 97 minutes are mostly work - shifts, errands, the arithmetic of a week. The endearment is the mother's word for the daughter, and it comes with a bill attached: care running upward, from child to parent, on a schedule with no unaccounted hours in it. The strain shows first in small administrative things. A shift swapped. A visit from the mother of the boy she likes.

They meet in group therapy and decide, quickly, that it is love. Both have schizophrenia, and Michael Rymer takes seriously what most romances keep in the background: that a couple here conducts its life alongside appointments, case workers, treatment plans, and relatives who have watched this sort of thing before. What they want is unremarkable. A flat in 1990s Australia, work, a plan, the ordinary permissions other adults are handed without applying for them. Two people, one flat, and a great many other people with opinions about both. The obstacle is not a villain but the terms of being well, which neither of them gets to negotiate. Australia's best actress award went to the lead performance, and the demand it answers is lucidity and its price, held in one scene without either being signalled.

The coast is the whole address: dunes, shallow water, a hut, weather that arrives without warning. Mike lives out there because his father has chosen to live away from people, an arrangement that leaves a boy with nobody his own age within walking distance. What he finds instead is a man living alone on the same stretch of shore, and pelicans with no parents left to feed them. A boy, a man, and a nest of birds, all of them left over from somebody else's arrangements. Henri Safran made it in Australia in 1977, 88 minutes, for families - which in practice means it refuses to hurry and lets the birds be birds, hand-fed, growing, following. The friendship across an enormous gap of age and circumstance is handled without commentary. So is whose decision the solitude was.

Angélique is sixty and still working nights, getting men to order another round in a cabaret by the French-German border. She likes the work, and that is the fact the film starts from and never apologises for: the drinking, the flirting, the late hours are not a trap she waits to be freed from but the shape of a life she chose and does well. The clients have thinned out, though. Sixty is late to be counting a night's takings. One of them, Michel, has been coming for years and now wants to marry her, and Marie Amachoukeli treats the offer as a real question rather than a rescue. What acceptance would cost - the room, the noise, the version of herself that exists only after dark - goes unmentioned in every scene and is plain in all of them.
